passage: Dear Samir, You asked how the meeting with Meenal's biodata went. On paper: good height, good job, the same community, and my mother glowing. I almost stopped reading at that point. But I met her four times in six weeks: two walks, one lunch with her sister, and one long evening when the bus broke down. She talks about her students the way some people talk about cricket. When I spilled my chai, she laughed, then wiped the neighbouring table too. She disagrees with me about money and says so plainly, and I trust that more than any number on the sheet. Neither of us mentioned height or caste even once. I would like to tell both families that we want to keep meeting. Write back and tell me if I'm being silly. Lokesh

qa.q: How many times did Lokesh meet Meenal over six weeks?
qa.a: Lokesh met her four times: two walks, a lunch with her sister and one long evening when the bus broke down.

qa.q: What does "tell me if I'm being silly" suggest Lokesh feels?
qa.a: Lokesh feels admiration and trust for Meenal but is a little unsure, wanting Samir's view before telling the families. 🙂

qa.q: Which choice by Lokesh gave a fuller picture than the biodata?
qa.a: Lokesh met Meenal several times in different settings and noticed how she treats people and how plainly she disagrees about money.

qa.q: How might Meenal have experienced those six weeks of meetings?
qa.a: Probably as time to be known as a person: she talked about her students, disagreed openly about money, and was not judged only by a list.

grounding: A young adult looks past the biodata's height, job and community to how the other person behaves over repeated meetings.

passage: Okay, so when Mummy handed me the biodata for Jatin, it said what they all say: height, salary, caste, hobbies, "fond of cooking". I told her I would talk to him before deciding anything. We spoke on three weekends, first on video, then on a walk by the lake. I asked how he handles a bad day. He said he goes quiet and then apologises; I said I go loud and then apologise; we both laughed. He asked follow-up questions and actually waited for the answers. He told me his sister disagrees with him on nearly everything and he likes it. None of that was on the sheet. I haven't said yes yet. But I'm deciding about a person, not a page. Disha

qa.q: How many weekends did Disha and Jatin talk?
qa.a: They spoke on three weekends, first on video and then on a walk by the lake.

qa.q: What is Disha feeling about Jatin, and what shows it?
qa.a: Disha feels hopeful and interested. They laughed together and Jatin listened, but Disha stays cautious because nothing is decided yet.

qa.q: What choice did Disha make on receiving the biodata, and what did it give?
qa.a: Disha asked to talk with Jatin before deciding anything. Over three weekends that showed things the sheet never did, such as how he handles a bad day and how he listens.

qa.q: What might Jatin have felt when Disha asked how he handles a bad day?
qa.a: Probably surprised and pleased to be asked about something real. His honest answer and the shared laugh suggest he felt at ease.

grounding: A young adult sets aside the biodata's list and learns about the other person through several long conversations.

passage:
My sister Sarita's biodata folder sat on our dining table for months. Every profile had the same columns: height, salary, caste, gotra, complexion. Papa sorted them into piles.
Harish's profile was in the "maybe" pile because his salary was lower. Sarita pulled it out anyway. I watched her meet him four times that summer. The first time, at a café, she asked him what made him angry. He thought about it and said, "Being lied to, and people who shout at waiters." She told me that on the auto ride home, grinning.
The third time, he came to our flat and helped Nani down the stairs without anyone asking. Sarita didn't say anything, but she kept looking at him.
I can't say exactly what she felt. But she stopped opening the folder after that.

qa.q: In which pile was Harish's profile?
qa.a: Harish's profile was in the "maybe" pile because his salary was lower.

qa.q: What might Sarita's grin on the auto ride suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she felt pleased and hopeful, because Harish's honest answer about waiters showed the kind of respect she cared about more than salary.

qa.q: What did Sarita's approach do well?
qa.a: She looked past the columns and used long talks and time with Harish to learn about his temper, his values and how he treats people like Nani and waiters.

qa.q: What would change if Sarita had only followed Papa's piles?
qa.a: She might never have met Harish, since his salary put him in the "maybe" pile, and she would have judged him only by the biodata columns.

grounding: It shows a young adult looking past biodata columns such as salary and caste to temperament and respect, learned through time together.

passage:
Monday. Vinita's mother handed her a printout: Raghav, twenty-four, six feet, government job, same community. "Perfect on paper," her mother said. Vinita folded it into her notebook and felt nothing at all.
Two weeks later, a Sunday. Vinita and Raghav walked around the lake for three hours. She asked how his family argued. He said, "Loudly, then we eat together." She told him she hated loud rooms. He paused. "Then I'd need to learn to argue softer. Could you teach me?" She laughed, surprised.
A month later, a Friday evening. Her mother asked, "So? Height, job, everything matches, na?" Vinita shook her head. "None of that is why I said yes to a fourth meeting, Ma. It's that he asked me to teach him something."

qa.q: How long did Vinita and Raghav walk around the lake?
qa.a: Vinita and Raghav walked around the lake for three hours.

qa.q: Why did Vinita feel nothing at all when she read the printout?
qa.a: The printout listed only height, job and community, so she felt bored and unmoved; none of it told her who Raghav really was.

qa.q: What went right in the Sunday walk, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Vinita asked about how his family handled arguments, and Raghav answered honestly and offered to change; that revealed his temperament and willingness to learn, which a printout can't show.

qa.q: How might Vinita's mother see the match differently from Vinita?
qa.a: Her mother sees the matching height, job and community as the main reasons, while Vinita values the respect and openness she found in their talks.

grounding: It shows, across three different days, a young adult moving from biodata facts to values and temperament learned through long talks.

passage:
Sit, Abhinav. You asked how I chose your grandfather, so I'll tell you properly.
I was a girl of twenty when the proposals started. My uncle brought a stack of horoscopes and photographs. One boy was a doctor, fair, tall; everyone was thrilled. I met him once. He talked for an hour about his car and never asked me a single question.
Your grandfather's proposal came later. Shorter, a clerk, and my aunt sniffed at that. But at our second meeting he asked what I was reading, and when I said poetry, he asked me to recite one. Then he listened, really listened.
I told my father, "I want more time with the clerk." Papa was surprised, but he allowed three more meetings. By the third, I knew.
Fifty years, Abhinav. Not once did he stop asking my opinion. That is what I, Aadhya, would look for again.

qa.q: What did the doctor talk about for an hour?
qa.a: The doctor talked for an hour about his car and never asked her a single question.

qa.q: How did Aadhya feel when the clerk asked her to recite a poem?
qa.a: She felt respected and interested, because he listened, really listened, which the doctor had not done.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Aadhya's story?
qa.a: The turning point was when she asked her father for more time with the clerk instead of choosing by the biodata; the extra meetings let her see his respect.

qa.q: How might Aadhya's aunt have seen the choice at the time?
qa.a: The aunt sniffed at a shorter clerk, so she probably saw it as settling for less, judging by job and looks rather than by how he treated Aadhya.

grounding: An elder recalls looking past height and profession in proposals to respect and temperament learned over several meetings.

passage:
The biodata Jagdish mama had sent listed it all: Rukhsar, five foot four, MSc, father a doctor, "fair, homely". Farhan, twenty-two, felt slightly sick reading it, as if they were shopping. When the families arranged a meeting at a Lucknow café, the power went out ten minutes in and the waiter apologised: no coffee, no fans. The families decided to wait in the car. Farhan and Rukhsar ended up walking under the dripping trees of the park across the road, umbrellas bumping.
They talked for two hours. About how she argued with her father over a stray dog. About his fear of letting his mother down. She asked how he treated waiters; he laughed and told her about the one he'd once shouted at, and how bad he felt. She liked that he admitted it. By the end he knew nothing new about her height or salary. He knew she was honest, quick-tempered and kind.

qa.q: What did the biodata say about Rukhsar's height?
qa.a: Five foot four.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel reading the biodata?
qa.a: He felt slightly sick and uncomfortable, as if they were shopping.

qa.q: Why did the long walk reveal more than the biodata?
qa.a: Talking for two hours showed values, temper and respect, like honesty about mistakes and how people treat others, which a list of qualities cannot.

qa.q: How might Rukhsar have seen Farhan after the walk?
qa.a: She seemed to respect him, liking that he admitted his mistake with the waiter instead of pretending to be perfect.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who looks past a biodata's height and qualifications to values, temperament and respect through long talk.
